items.q: How does the brain know when you need salt or water?
items.a: The **OVLT** sits behind a weak blood-brain barrier fence and senses bloodstream **osmolarity** and blood pressure, then drives thirst, **vasopressin**, and kidney retention or excretion.

items.q: What's the difference between osmotic and hypovolemic thirst?
items.a: **Osmotic thirst**: high salt → drink water while vasopressin **restricts urine**. **Hypovolemic thirst**: low blood volume/pressure → seek **water plus salt**. Both gate fluid balance, not just "feeling thirsty."

items.q: Is there one right daily sodium target?
items.a: No — **context decides**. Population data links ~**2.3 g sodium/day** with lower CV risk; risk rises above ~**4–5 g**. Hypertensive people must be cautious; **know your blood pressure first**.

items.q: When might higher salt intake help instead of hurt?
items.a: Low BP, dizziness on standing, **POTS**, orthostatic hypotension, or idiopathic orthostatic tachycardia may benefit from about **6–10 g salt/day** (**2,400–4,000 mg sodium**) per the ASH guidance cited.

items.q: How much fluid during exercise or hard cognitive work?
items.a: Use the **Galpin equation**: body weight (lb) ÷ **30** = ounces of fluid every **15 minutes**. Most people under-hydrate **and** under-electrolyte; sweat loss of **1–5 lb/hour** hits mental and physical capacity.

items.q: Why do low-carb diets and stress change salt needs?
items.a: Low-carb increases excretion of **water, sodium, and potassium** — replenish deliberately. Stress links via **aldosterone/glucocorticoids** to salt craving; **too little sodium impairs the stress response**.

items.q: Why do salty-sweet processed foods make you overeat?
items.a: Parallel salty/sweet pathways in mouth and gut normally self-limit; the **salty-sweet combo masks satiety**. Dial salt on an **unprocessed food background** so true appetite can speak; more salt may cut sugar cravings.

items.q: Can drinking too much water be dangerous?
items.a: Yes — **hyponatremia**: over-water dilutes sodium → brain dysfunction, and can be **fatal**. Sodium is also essential for **neuronal action potentials** — brain function depends on it.
